tooltips.key: The secret key. Every letter of the message is shifted by the matching key letter; the key repeats over the whole message.
tooltips.alphabet: The set of letters the cipher works with. Paste any letters — the tool uppercases them and drops duplicates. The default is the English alphabet.
tooltips.unknownKey: Check this if you do not know the key. A guided cracker opens below: it helps you find the key length and then every key letter, step by step.
tooltips.hintPresets: How much help the cracker gives you. Easy shows every hint; Hard hides most of them so you can practise.

toggle.highlightRepeats: Colours repeated letter groups in the text — the distances between them hint at the key length.
toggle.showGaps: Shows the distances between repeated sequences, next to each group.
toggle.confidenceBars: Shows a confidence bar and a plain-language reason on each key length card.
toggle.englishReference: Draws the English letter frequencies over the slice bars, so you can align them by eye.
toggle.matchScore: Shows how closely the current alignment matches English letter frequencies, in percent.
toggle.mostLikelyGlow: Gently highlights the alignment that matches English best.
toggle.livePreview: Decrypts the text live while you pick key letters: letters of set slices appear, the rest stay as underscores.
toggle.cribs: Shows a panel where you can guess a word from the plaintext and get key letters from it.

tooltips.keyLengthCards: Likely key lengths ranked by two signals: distances between repeated sequences, and how English-like the text slices look. Click a card to choose.
tooltips.otherLength: Enter a key length manually if none of the suggested cards fits.
tooltips.sliceTabs: With a key length of N the text splits into N slices; every letter of a slice is shifted by the same key letter. Click a tab to work on that slice.
tooltips.chartArrows: Rotate the slice bars against the English reference. At the best alignment the shown letter is the key letter — it is applied immediately, watch the preview.
tooltips.matchScore: How closely the current alignment matches English letter frequencies, in percent. Higher is better.
tooltips.keyStrip: Your key as you build it. Click a cell to jump to its slice, type a letter to override the chart choice, clear a cell to un-set it.
tooltips.cribInput: If you guess a word that appears in the plaintext, the cracker computes which key letters it implies, at every position it fits.
tooltips.apply: Fill the empty key slots with the letters this position suggests. Letters already set differently are never overwritten.
tooltips.back: Return to the previous step. Your choices are kept.
tooltips.next: Continue to the next step once this step is complete.
tooltips.skip: Close the cracker and enter the key manually.
tooltips.useThisKey: Fill the key field with the key you assembled and decrypt the message with it.

vigenere.description: Each letter of the message is shifted by the matching letter of a repeating key.
vigenere.origin: Described by Giovan Battista Bellaso in 1553, later misattributed to Blaise de Vigenère.

controls.rotate-left: the left arrow under the discs
controls.rotate-right: the right arrow under the discs

vigenere.1467: Leon Battista Alberti invents the cipher disk — the first idea of using several alphabets.
vigenere.1508: Johannes Trithemius publishes the tabula recta, a table of all letter shifts.
vigenere.1553: Giovan Battista Bellaso describes the repeating-key cipher with an easy-to-remember key phrase.
vigenere.1586: Blaise de Vigenère publishes a similar cipher; the repeating-key scheme is later misattributed to him.
vigenere.1863: Friedrich Kasiski publishes a general method for finding the key length (Charles Babbage had broken it privately a decade earlier).
vigenere.1920s: William Friedman develops the index of coincidence, making the attack statistical and rigorous.

caesar.121: Suetonius describes both Caesar's shift of 3 and Augustus' shift of 1 in The Lives of the Twelve Caesars.
caesar.800: Al-Kindi writes on decrypting messages by letter frequency, breaking every single-alphabet substitution cipher.
caesar.1553: Bellaso's repeating-key cipher — "many Caesars", one per key letter — makes fixed shifts obsolete.
caesar.58bc: Julius Caesar uses a shift of 3 for private correspondence, his biographer Suetonius reports.

alberti.1467: Leon Battista Alberti presents the cipher disk in De Cifris — the first idea of using several alphabets.
alberti.1508: Johannes Trithemius publishes the tabula recta, a square table of all alphabets, extending the disk idea.
alberti.1553: Giovan Battista Bellaso turns the alphabets with a repeating key phrase — the scheme later called the Vigenère cipher.

vigenere-easy-1.title: Break a message from the novel
vigenere-easy-1.hint2: The key is a common pet: three letters.

vigenere-easy-2.title: The novel continues
vigenere-easy-2.hint2: The key is a citrus fruit.

vigenere-medium-1.title: A truth universally acknowledged
vigenere-medium-1.hint2: The key is a fruit again — six letters this time.

vigenere-medium-2.title: Once upon a midnight dreary
vigenere-medium-2.hint2: The key names the bird of the poem.

vigenere-hard-1.title: To be or not to be
vigenere-hard-1.hint1: The key length is 11 — frequency hints get shaky, a crib is safer.
vigenere-hard-1.hint2: The key is a songbird that sings at night.
vigenere-hard-1.hint3: The word TOBE appears at the very start — place it as a crib.

vigenere-hard-2.title: Four score and seven
vigenere-hard-2.hint1: The key length is 10 — use a crib.
vigenere-hard-2.hint2: The key is an adjective meaning impossible to decode.
vigenere-hard-2.hint3: The opening FOURSCORE works as a crib.

caesar-easy-1.title: Fear itself
caesar-easy-1.hint1: The shift is the classic one — the number Caesar himself used.
caesar-easy-1.hint2: The shift is 3: THE becomes WKH.

caesar-medium-1.title: Eliminate the impossible
caesar-medium-1.hint1: Frequency analysis: the most frequent ciphertext letter is the encrypted E.
caesar-medium-1.hint2: The shift is 11 — count the letters: E becomes P.

caesar-hard-1.title: Friends, Romans, countrymen
caesar-hard-1.hint1: The shift is 23 — small enough to walk through by hand.
caesar-hard-1.hint2: The ciphertext hides the start of a famous Roman speech.

alberti-easy-1.title: I came, I saw, I conquered
alberti-easy-1.hint1: The disc turns after every 2 letters — the period is 2.
alberti-easy-1.hint2: The step is 3, and the discs start at their default alignment; reload the page if you turned them.

alberti-medium-1.title: Per aspera ad astra
alberti-medium-1.hint2: The step is 4 — after every chunk the inner disc jumps four positions.

alberti-hard-1.title: All Gaul
alberti-hard-1.hint3: It is the opening of Julius Caesar's Gallic War — written with the 20 letters of Alberti's disc only.

tooltips.swap: Swap the two sides: the tool switches between encrypting and decrypting. The current mode shows in the header.

caesar.rotation: The shift: every letter of the message moves this many positions forward through the alphabet (backwards in decrypt mode).
caesar.keepSpaces: Keep spaces: preserve the word layout instead of dropping all spaces.
caesar.keepCase: Keep case: preserve capital letters instead of writing everything in capitals.

tooltips.alphabet: The alphabet the cipher works on: pick a preset or paste your own ordered letters.

alberti.disc: Alberti's cipher disk: the fixed outer disc holds the plaintext alphabet, the movable inner disc holds the mixed ciphertext alphabet.
alberti.increment: The turn step: how many positions the inner disc jumps after every chunk of the period.
alberti.period: The period: how many letters are encrypted before the inner disc turns.

caesar.description: Every letter of the message is shifted by the same fixed number of positions in the alphabet.
caesar.origin: Named after Julius Caesar, who reportedly used a shift of 3 in private correspondence.

alberti.description: The first polyalphabetic cipher: two rotating discs switch alphabets every few letters.
alberti.origin: Devised by Leon Battista Alberti around 1467 on his cipher disk, Formula.

plaintext.name: Plaintext
plaintext.definition: The original readable message before encryption.

ciphertext.name: Ciphertext
ciphertext.definition: The scrambled message produced by encryption.

cryptogram.name: Cryptogram
cryptogram.definition: A message written in cipher; on this site it also names the input field.

key.name: Key
key.definition: The secret that controls how the text is scrambled.

alphabet.name: Alphabet
alphabet.definition: The set of letters the cipher works with.

key-length.name: Key length
key-length.definition: How many letters the key has before it starts repeating.

shift.name: Shift
shift.definition: How far a letter moves along the alphabet.

substitution.name: Substitution
substitution.definition: Replacing each letter with another one.

polyalphabetic.name: Polyalphabetic
polyalphabetic.definition: A cipher that uses several alphabets in turn instead of one.

slice.name: Slice
slice.definition: Every Nth letter of the text (N = key length). All letters of one slice are shifted by the same key letter.

frequency-analysis.name: Frequency analysis
frequency-analysis.definition: Studying how often letters appear; comparing the counts with the language reveals the plaintext.

index-of-coincidence.name: Index of coincidence
index-of-coincidence.definition: A number (about 0.067 for English) showing how likely two random letters of a text are equal.

kasiski-examination.name: Kasiski examination
kasiski-examination.definition: Finding the key length from the distances between repeated sequences in the ciphertext.

crib.name: Crib
crib.definition: A word you guess is in the plaintext; comparing it with the ciphertext reveals key letters.

brute-force.name: Brute force
brute-force.definition: Trying every possible key until the message makes sense; possible only when the key space is small.

period.name: Period
period.definition: How many letters are encrypted before the disc or alphabet changes; after each period the substitution starts over.
